facts.text: The Annihilators' tagline: "For them, the Vietnam War wasn't Hell... it was Practice."
The Vietnam jungle scenes were shot first, near Charlie Brown airport in Atlanta, Georgia, long before the film moved on to the city streets.
This was shot in Atlanta at the same time as Chuck Norris' Invasion U.S.A. (1985). Locations and stunt men were shared: crews did this by day, then Norris' film at night.
Andy Wood, who plays squad demolitions man Woody, also appeared in Rambo: First Blood Part II (1985), another Vietnam-vet action film released the same year.

During this booby-trap patrol, Gerrit Graham (Ray Track) was hurt for real: a plastic canteen stand-in made a spiked log bounce into his forehead. He needed microsurgery, and the script was rewritten.
Overseas, The Annihilators was sold as Action Force in Europe, a title that sounds more like a toy line than a grindhouse vigilante flick.
Gerrit Graham (Ray Track) later became a writer on VH1's Pop Up Video, the very show this bubble style is borrowed from.
The grocery store at the heart of the neighborhood is Little's Food Store, a real Cabbagetown, Atlanta location per a Good Efficient Butchery review.
Roy Boy Jagger is played by Paul Koslo, who'd earlier been in The Omega Man (1971) and Vanishing Point (1971), and later Robot Jox (1989).
In the UK, two seconds were cut for an 18 rating: a shot of a bare-breasted woman being stabbed, removed as sexualized violence.
Director Charles E. Sellier Jr. made this a year after Silent Night, Deadly Night (1984), the notorious Christmas slasher about a killer Santa.
Christopher Stone (Bill "Sarge" Ecker) co-starred with his wife Dee Wallace in The Howling and Cujo. He died of a heart attack at 53, in 1995.
The film's grocery-store victim is killed with a meat tenderizer, the kind sold in his own shop. A blog review at Good Efficient Butchery noted the grim irony.
Sid Conrad (Louie Nace) served in the U.S. Army at the Battle of the Bulge, then earned a Columbia journalism master's on the G.I. Bill before becoming a TV character actor.
The budget forced the writers to shrink the group of Vietnam vets assembling here to just four.
Lieutenant Hawkins is played by Jim Antonio, the older brother of actor-director Lou Antonio.
Gerrit Graham (Ray Track) was best known for Brian De Palma films like Phantom of the Paradise (1974), and starred opposite Kurt Russell in Used Cars (1980).
A Good Efficient Butchery review compared Paul Koslo's mulleted, cartoonish gang boss Roy Boy Jagger to Gavan O'Herlihy's villain Fraker in Death Wish 3.
Atlanta's Cabbagetown district stood in for the film's fictional gang-ridden neighborhood, South Point.
It rode the Vietnam-vet vigilante wave of Taxi Driver, Rolling Thunder, The Exterminator and First Blood, with a Seven Samurai-style team-up twist.
Andrew Skeates of Blueprint Review called it a grown-up take on The A-Team, where the bad guys die in bloody, squib-popping fashion instead of just crashing their vans.
Paul Koslo (Roy Boy Jagger) was born Manfred Koslowski in Germany and raised in Saskatchewan, Canada, after his soldier father moved the family post-WWII.
Lawrence Hilton-Jacobs (Garrett Floyd) was the only cast member to appear in all 95 episodes of Welcome Back, Kotter, as Freddie "Boom Boom" Washington.
Lawrence Hilton-Jacobs (Garrett Floyd) was also in the classic Cooley High (1975) and Claudine (1974), the same era as his Welcome Back, Kotter fame.
Unlike typical movie gangs, the punks here are played by men in their 30s and 40s, not teens, as a Good Efficient Butchery review pointed out.
Despite all the shootouts, bullet holes never appear in the red panel van, a continuity slip.
After Gerrit Graham's on-set forehead injury, his role was rewritten and cut down. He returned only in the final week of shooting to film his reduced scenes.
Director Charles E. Sellier Jr. created the 1970s book and NBC series The Life and Times of Grizzly Adams, a long way from this violent Atlanta vigilante flick.
Sarah Morgan of ON Magazine described director Charles E. Sellier Jr. as a "low-rent Roger Corman" who mentored young writers, producers and directors on even smaller budgets.
Gerrit Graham (Ray Track) wrote the lyrics to the Grateful Dead song "Victim or the Crime," set to a tune by Bob Weir.
The Annihilators was a cable late-night staple: USA Network's Up All Night aired it on April 15, October 11 and November 25, 1989.
Director Charles E. Sellier Jr.'s Sunn Classic Pictures run produced eleven features that rank among the top 100 highest-grossing independent films, per Wikipedia.
New World Pictures released it regionally in summer 1985. It was still reaching theaters like one in Toledo, Ohio, by January 1986.
This was the last film Charles E. Sellier Jr. directed. He died in 2011 at age 67 in Idaho.
The Annihilators is name-checked in the 2019 documentary Our VHS Collection.
